stages.name: Labour market indicators
stages.title: Labour market indicators
stages.sub: Read the employment rate, unemployment rate, inactivity rate and under-employment, and judge what changes in them actually mean.

steps.q: A country has 50 million people aged 16 to 64. To work out a labour market rate, who do we compare against?
steps.hint: Retired people and children are not usually counted in labour statistics.
steps.pre: Rates are calculated as a share of the

steps.q: Of the working-age population, some are in a job, whether full-time, part-time or self-employed. What does that share tell you?
steps.right: How many working-age people are in a job
steps.wrong: How many working-age people are looking for a job
steps.hint: This is about people who already have work, not people searching for it.

steps.q: Now take working-age people who are economically active but have no job. What does their share of the working-age population show?
steps.right: How many are jobless but still seeking work
steps.wrong: How many have simply given up looking for work
steps.hint: Economically active means willing and able to work, not that they have found it yet.
steps.pre: That share, measured by the Labour Force Survey, is the

steps.q: Some working-age people are neither in a job nor unemployed because they aren't seeking work, like students and carers. What does their share capture?
steps.right: Those not working and not looking for work
steps.wrong: Those working part-time instead of full-time
steps.hint: These people are outside the labour force entirely, not searching for a job.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: A part-timer wants full-time hours but finds only 15 a week. Do employment, unemployment and inactivity rates capture this?
steps.right: No, they miss it because this worker counts as employed
steps.wrong: Yes, this worker is correctly recorded as unemployed
steps.hint: The three rates only ask whether someone has a job, not whether they have enough hours or the right job.

steps.q: The unemployment rate falls, the inactivity rate rises by almost as much, and employment barely moves. Is the labour market actually healthier?
steps.right: Not necessarily, people may have left the labour force rather than found jobs
steps.wrong: Yes, because unemployment falling always means more people are working
steps.hint: Falling unemployment on its own does not tell you where those people went, into jobs or out of the workforce.
